blocks.text: 1. Weight Decay
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072419-422664895.png

L2 Regularization, already covered in its own topic, introduced adding a penalty to the loss based on the sum of squared weights. Weight Decay is the name for the exact same idea, viewed from the optimizer's own perspective instead.

Rather than describing a penalty added to the loss, Weight Decay describes the practical update behavior it produces: shrinking every weight slightly on each training update, covered in full depth throughout this topic.
2. The Connection To L2 Regularization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072420-232413960.png

This connects directly back to the Weight Decay Connection already covered inside L2 Regularization's own topic. L2's penalty gradient is proportional to the weight itself, a fact already established there.

Subtracting that gradient during each update looks exactly like multiplying the weight by a number slightly less than 1, which is precisely why this practical effect earned its own distinctive name, Weight Decay.

blocks.text: 3. The Update Rule View

This connects back to Gradient Descent, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. The plain update subtracts the loss gradient scaled by the learning rate, exactly as already covered there.

Weight Decay adds one more small subtraction to that same update: the weight itself, scaled by the decay rate, a genuinely simple, direct addition to the update rule already familiar from that earlier module.
4. Exact Equivalence Under Plain SGD
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072420-514057735.png

A genuinely important mathematical fact: for plain Stochastic Gradient Descent, already covered in its own topic, L2 Regularization and Weight Decay are genuinely, exactly mathematically equivalent, two different ways of describing the identical update.

This equivalence is why the two terms are so often used interchangeably in casual conversation, even though, as the next section covers, this equivalence genuinely breaks down for more advanced optimizers.
5. A Genuine Divergence Under Adam
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072420-700625783.png

A genuinely important, subtler fact follows. For Adam, already covered in its own topic, with its adaptive per-weight learning rates, L2 Regularization and Weight Decay are genuinely NOT exactly equivalent anymore.

Adam's adaptive scaling interacts with the L2 penalty gradient in a way that genuinely distorts its intended shrinkage effect, a subtle but genuinely real problem that motivated the very next topic covered in this section.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: This divergence under Adam is not a minor theoretical footnote. It genuinely affects how well regularization works in practice, which is exactly why AdamW, already covered in its own topic, exists as a direct fix.

blocks.text: 6. Why AdamW Exists
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072420-339608717.png

This connects directly back to AdamW, already covered in its own topic within the Backpropagation & Optimization module. AdamW was specifically designed to apply Weight Decay directly and correctly, addressing the divergence already covered in the previous section.

Rather than relying on the L2-penalty version that behaves subtly differently under Adam's adaptive updates, AdamW applies the weight-shrinking update directly, decoupled from the adaptive gradient scaling entirely.
7. The Decay Rate Hyperparameter
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072421-560469558.png

This uses the same kind of hyperparameter already covered as lambda in L1 and L2 Regularization, here commonly called the decay rate. A larger decay rate produces stronger shrinkage on every single update.
A smaller decay rate produces weaker shrinkage instead, keeping training closer to plain, unregularized behavior, tunable through the same Hyperparameter Tuning process covered later in this course.
8. Connecting Back to Bias-Variance

This connects back to the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Weight Decay deliberately increases bias slightly, since it constrains the model away from perfectly fitting the training data.

This happens in direct exchange for a genuinely larger reduction in variance, exactly the same deliberate tradeoff already covered for L1 and L2 Regularization, just described here in terms of the update rule rather than the loss.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When To Think In Terms Of Weight Decay

blocks.alt: Recognizing When To Think In Terms Of Weight Decay
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445072421-316554372.png

Using Adam or AdamW, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module, is a direct case where the distinction from L2 Regularization, already covered in this topic, genuinely matters for correct behavior.

Using plain Gradient Descent or plain Stochastic Gradient Descent is a genuine case where Weight Decay and L2 Regularization are genuinely interchangeable terms, since the equivalence already covered in this topic holds exactly.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates the genuine equivalence between an L2 penalty gradient step and a direct Weight Decay update step, confirming the mathematical fact already covered in this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

weight = 2.0
learning_rate = 0.1
decay_rate = 0.01  # already covered as the decay rate hyperparameter in this topic
loss_gradient = 0.5  # the gradient of the plain loss with respect to this weight, ignoring regularization

# Approach 1: L2 Regularization, already covered in its own topic
# The L2 penalty gradient is proportional to the weight itself, already covered as the connection in this topic
l2_penalty_gradient = 2 * decay_rate * weight
combined_gradient = loss_gradient + l2_penalty_gradient
weight_after_l2 = weight - learning_rate * combined_gradient

# Approach 2: Weight Decay applied directly, already covered as the update rule view in this topic
weight_after_decay_step = weight - learning_rate * loss_gradient
weight_after_decay_step = weight_after_decay_step - learning_rate * 2 * decay_rate * weight

print(f"Weight after L2 Regularization approach: {weight_after_l2:.6f}")
print(f"Weight after direct Weight Decay approach: {weight_after_decay_step:.6f}")
print("Under plain SGD, both approaches produce a genuinely identical result, exactly the equivalence already covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This equivalence, already covered in this topic, only holds for plain gradient-based updates. Under Adam's adaptive scaling, already covered in its own topic, these two approaches genuinely produce different results.

blocks.text: 11. Regularization Techniques: Progress Recap

items: Weight Decay is the name for L2 Regularization's effect, viewed from the optimizer's own update-rule perspective.
Its update subtracts the weight itself, scaled by the decay rate, on every single training step.
Under plain SGD, L2 Regularization and Weight Decay are exactly mathematically equivalent.
Under Adam, this equivalence genuinely breaks down due to Adam's adaptive per-weight learning rates.
AdamW was specifically designed to apply Weight Decay directly and correctly under Adam's adaptive updates.
The decay rate hyperparameter controls shrinkage strength, the same kind of knob already covered in L1 and L2 Regularization.
It deliberately trades a small amount of increased bias for a genuinely larger reduction in variance.
The distinction from L2 Regularization genuinely matters when using Adam or AdamW, but not under plain SGD.
Next up: Gradient Clipping, the module's final regularization technique, which works by constraining gradient magnitude directly rather than the weights.
